addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied — one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level — the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference — a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade → jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", …)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init — stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in
[refactor-20260716.md](notes/refactor-20260716.md).

Program ladder — one rung per cycle (adjacent stages
consolidated 2026-07-24; rung titles are the anticipated
close-out commit titles; unshipped versions are provisional —
jj-lib may split into two cycles). Shipped-rung refs point at
close-out commits on `refactor-vc-x1`, treated as permanent:
the branch is long-lived and lands on main merge-only, never
rebased.

what happens post-squash:

- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a
  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.
- **Finalize the chores section** (opened during Preparation
  and grown per commit — see [Chores sections](#chores-sections)):
  - The problem statement is already the chores intro (written
    when the section was opened) and the plan ladder is already
    the `### As-built ladder` (a rung appended per commit), so
    close-out only *finalizes*, it does not cut-and-paste.
  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title if the
    cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor back-reference.
  - Add any `### design subsections`; optional `### Outcome`
    notes.
  - Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block with
    `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).

Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time —
see [Pushing](#pushing).

## Numbering

Each commit's phase is encoded in the version suffix — `-0`
Preparation, `-1`/`-2`/… Work, bare `X.Y.Z` Close-out,
recursively for sub-cycles. The full scheme — disambiguation,
nesting, optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
format, and the per-phase bump — lives in
[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering), which is the
single source of truth for this repo's versioning.

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
through:

1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
   root).
2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
   for the loop-and-squash technique).
3. **Flip this commit `(current)` → `(done)`** in `## In
   Progress` — before the cargo cycle and the commit.
4. **Validate the artifact** — a medium-specific step, skip-able
   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
   example the cargo cycle is:
   1. `cargo fmt`
   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
   3. `cargo test`
   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)

   tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
   changes and we iterate until complete.
6. **Write the commit description** — see

   commit stages commit both repos and stamp the `ochid:`
   trailers. Never pre-commit the rung with `jj commit`: an
   empty `@` at push mints a stamped empty duplicate
   (bugs.md #6). Push approval is per-push — step 7's
   review covers it only when the user's go explicitly
   includes the push.

**Two overrides apply:**

- **Deviation or question** — any time the work deviates
  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
  surface it; don't push through.
- **ESC-ESC** — the user can interrupt at any point to pull
  a review or question forward.

[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):

  leading-`/`-means-root special case). Docs recommend
  relative; absolute is allowed but discouraged, since it
  commits one machine's layout.
- The identical-block invariant cannot survive
  file-relative values (the same bytes mean different dirs
  on each side), so it is replaced by **resolved
  agreement** — canonicalize each side's declared pair and
  require both files to name the same two directories. The
  0.75.0-3 coherence preflight keeps its role, comparing
  reality instead of spelling.
- Side detection: the entry resolving to the config's own
  directory names the side (`work = "."` → work repo).
  Repos need not be nested.
- ochid trailer prefixes become opaque registry labels
  resolved through `[repos]`, not filesystem spellings: `/`
  and `/.claude` stay valid as historical labels for
  work/bot, so published trailers keep resolving. Labels are
  intended to grow into URLs — the local-path half of the
  Todo "ochid: bot-repo location qualifier", whose published
  half lives in
  [forks-multi-user.md](../forks-multi-user.md#per-user-bot-repos-via-url-shaped-ochid).

  topology because the schema is unreleased and freshly

  - consequence worth knowing — where the identity check
    happens moved, and it caught a latent defect. See
    [Identity enforcement: git commits, jj pushes](#identity-enforcement-git-commits-jj-pushes)

### Identity enforcement: git commits, jj pushes

Swapping init's publish path from `git push` to `jj git push`
moved *when* a missing user identity is caught, which surfaced
as two CLI-fixture tests failing at the new push step. The two
tools enforce at opposite ends:

- **git — at commit.** `git commit` with no `user.name` /
  `user.email` tries to synthesize one from
  `username@hostname`; if that isn't usable it refuses
  outright (`fatal: unable to auto-detect email address (got
  'wink@3900x.(none)')`). Nothing is checked at push time —
  `git push` never inspects an existing commit's author.
- **jj — at push.** `jj commit` succeeds with an explicit
  *empty identity*, warning `Name and email not configured.
  Until configured, your commits will be created with the
  empty identity, and can't be pushed to remotes.` The
  enforcement lands at `jj git push`: `Error: Won't push
  commit <id> since it has no author and/or committer set`.

We think jj's split follows from its model: local commits are
cheap and rewritable, so it defers the check to the boundary
where history becomes shared and permanent.

The latent defect: init already used `jj commit` for the
initial commit, so under the old flow the CLI fixtures — whose
`HOME` is an isolated tempdir with no user config — produced
empty-identity commits and `git push` shipped them to the bare

content.content:
322	## Pushing
323	
324	### Policy
325	
326	Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
327	progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out** —
328	the cycle's result must be published.
329	
330	**Approval is per-push.** Every push — any repo, any kind:
331	cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push —
332	happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
333	published and explicitly approved that specific push.
334	Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
335	the push itself; stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.
336	
337	**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
338	the gates.** The gates above — per-push approval, the
339	commit-description review (show title+body and stop), and the
340	hard stop after push/squash-push — are the *interactive
341	default*.
342	They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
343	bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
344	and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
345	through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
346	continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:
347	
348	- **Explicit grant** — never inferred from a task merely being
349	  well-scoped; the user's words must authorize unattended
350	  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
351	  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
352	  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
353	  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
354	  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
355	  unattended") waives them.
356	- **Bounded goal** — covers the named task only; does not carry
357	  to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
358	- **Destructive ops still pause** — delegation covers the task's
359	  ordinary commits and pushes; it does *not* pre-authorize a
360	  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
361	  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
362	  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
363	  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
364	  reaches this.
365	- **Still transparent** — report each commit/push as it lands
366	  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
367	- **When in doubt, ask** — ambiguous authorization falls back to
368	  per-push approval.
369	
370	### Shape at close-out push
371	
372	At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
373	shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
374	the options and get user approval before pushing — once on
375	the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
376	needs approval), so choose deliberately.
377	
378	- **Squash to one commit** — single entry on the target.
379	  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
380	  focused on one or two files.
381	- **Merge non-ff** *(current default)* — `main` gains a
382	  merge commit (`X.Y.Z`); cycle commits stay reachable via
383	  two parents. `jj log -r ..@ -n <N>` shows the trapezoidal
384	  shape. See [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe)
385	  for the full setup sequence.
386	- **Keep separate** — one commit per cycle entry on
387	  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
388	  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
389	  `Commits:` ref; no consolidation churn.
390	
391	Set up squash/merge before invoking `vc-x1 push`; use
392	`jj git push` directly for non-standard shapes.
393	
394	### Merge non-ff recipe
395	
396	Setting up a [Merge non-ff](#shape-at-close-out-push)
397	close-out is a fixed sequence. `<closeout>` is the cycle's
398	close-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out
399	(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last
400	Work commit:
401	
402	1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge** — `jj rebase -r
403	   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.
404	   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.
405	   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).
406	   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.
407	
408	   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of
409	   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.
410	2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the
411	   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing
412	   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;
413	   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.
414	3. **Push** — `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.

## Pushing

### Policy

Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out** —
the cycle's result must be published.

**Approval is per-push.** Every push — any repo, any kind:
cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push —
happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
published and explicitly approved that specific push.
Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
the push itself; stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.

**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
the gates.** The gates above — per-push approval, the
commit-description review (show title+body and stop), and the
hard stop after push/squash-push — are the *interactive
default*.
They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:

- **Explicit grant** — never inferred from a task merely being
  well-scoped; the user's words must authorize unattended
  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
  unattended") waives them.
- **Bounded goal** — covers the named task only; does not carry
  to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
- **Destructive ops still pause** — delegation covers the task's
  ordinary commits and pushes; it does *not* pre-authorize a
  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
  reaches this.
- **Still transparent** — report each commit/push as it lands
  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
- **When in doubt, ask** — ambiguous authorization falls back to
  per-push approval.

### Shape at close-out push

At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
the options and get user approval before pushing — once on
the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
needs approval), so choose deliberately.

- **Squash to one commit** — single entry on the target.
  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
  focused on one or two files.
- **Merge non-ff** *(current default)* — `main` gains a
  merge commit (`X.Y.Z`); cycle commits stay reachable via
  two parents. `jj log -r ..@ -n <N>` shows the trapezoidal
  shape. See [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe)
  for the full setup sequence.
- **Keep separate** — one commit per cycle entry on
  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
  `Commits:` ref; no consolidation churn.

Set up squash/merge before invoking `vc-x1 push`; use
`jj git push` directly for non-standard shapes.

### Merge non-ff recipe

Setting up a [Merge non-ff](#shape-at-close-out-push)
close-out is a fixed sequence. `<closeout>` is the cycle's
close-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out
(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last
Work commit:

1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge** — `jj rebase -r
   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.
   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.
   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).
   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.

   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of
   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.
2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the
   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing
   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;
   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.
3. **Push** — `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.

**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are
immutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the
push force-updates `main`.
The standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*
the close-out push.

### vc-x1 push wrapper

`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).

**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md` —
this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.

### .claude cadence

**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
with every work-repo commit in that push.

The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
across the cycle; its change ID stays stable across
snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.

`.claude` is a linear journal — all session work lives
on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
work-repo branches** — risks the bot steering session
pushes to the wrong remote ref.

Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
session information created, which we don't worry about.
The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
remain empty.

### Bot communication at the reviews

Use plain prose — no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
"Checkpoint N", etc.):

- Only the `####` cycle block goes — the `###` program heading and its ladder stay put (0.76.0 flipped to `(done)`, 0.77.0 becomes the next rung), because the program isn't finished; three more cycles follow.

We think jj's split follows from its model: local commits are
cheap and rewritable, so it defers the check to the boundary
where history becomes shared and permanent.

The latent defect: init already used `jj commit` for the
initial commit, so under the old flow the CLI fixtures — whose
`HOME` is an isolated tempdir with no user config — produced
empty-identity commits and `git push` shipped them to the bare
remotes without complaint. Nothing verified authorship, so it
went unnoticed. The jj-only path fails loudly instead, which is
why `CliFixture::new` now seeds a `[user]` identity: not test
scaffolding for its own sake, but the fixture finally supplying
what a real workspace always has.

Not documented upstream: jj's config, git-compatibility, and
FAQ pages don't mention the empty identity or the push-time
refusal (checked 2026-07-27) — jj's runtime warning and error
text are the authoritative statement.

### Outcome

- Shipped in five Work rungs on `refactor-vc-x1`.
  `.vc-config.toml` names repos instead of describing a
  filesystem: `[repos]` maps labels to ordinary paths, each
  side's file states its own view, and coherence is checked
  against resolved directories (plus self-identification)
  rather than identical bytes. ochid prefixes became canonical
  side labels, so a workspace may name its bot dir anything
  and still read/write `/.claude` trailers.
- De-gitify init rode as the last rung and paid for itself
  twice: bugs.md #1 and #2 fixed, both of whose workarounds
  came out of `tests/cli_sync.rs`, and `push_repo`'s
  `clean_exclude` parameter deleted with the `git clean` it
  existed to survive.
- Legacy handling is deliberately concentrated in
  `src/legacy_vc_config.rs` — two pre-`[repos]` generations
  read at the bootstrap surfaces only (clone, validate-desc /
  fix-desc's `--other-repo`), every other resolver rejecting
  with a rewrite hint. Retirement is a module delete plus the

  `.vc-config.toml` names repos instead of describing a
  filesystem: `[repos]` maps labels to ordinary paths, each
  side's file states its own view, and coherence is checked

  rather than identical bytes. ochid prefixes became canonical
  side labels, so a workspace may name its bot dir anything

Yes, I want to make it a trapezoidal commit on this branch,
as we've done on 0.73.0, 0.74.0 and 0.75.0. And I want to use
`vc-x1-dev push ..` to push both repos with the same descriptor.
Since vc-x1-dev doesn't quite yet support trapezoidal commit,
the intent that is the next task 0.77.0, so we'll have to do
some of it "manually".

Let's review that technique so we're on the same page.

vc-x1-dev 0.76.0

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main` — one resumable command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (tracking / bot-published / sync checks —
no build steps; run project checks yourself before pushing)
→ review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-work → commit-bot (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(work repo → <bookmark>, bot repo → main) → push-work →
squash-push-bot. Failures in commit-work / commit-bot /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-work.
After push-work succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1-dev push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (flag form; see positional)

  -V, --version
          Print the `vc-x1 X.Y.Z` banner as the first line, then continue. With
          no subcommand, prints the banner and exits.
          
          Replaces clap's auto-version (which would exit after printing): the
          banner now rides along with normal subcommand execution rather than
          gating it, so scripts can capture the version *and* the command's
          output in one invocation.

      --restart
          Clear any saved state file and start from stage 1

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --from <STAGE>
          Explicit stage to jump to (advanced / debug use)

          Possible values:
          - preflight:       Verify bookmark tracking, the bot-published
            invariant, and sync state
          - review:          Present diff for the first approval gate
          - message:         Compose / edit the commit message; present for
            second gate
          - commit-work:     Commit the work repo
          - commit-bot:      Commit the `.claude` bot repo (skipped if empty)
          - bookmark-set:    Advance each repo's bookmark to its `@-`: work →
            `<bookmark>`, bot → `main`
          - push-work:       `jj git push --bookmark <b> -R .`
          - squash-push-bot: In-process squash of `.claude`'s trailing session
            writes + push `main`

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --status
          Print where the saved state thinks we are and exit

      --recheck
          Re-run `preflight` even on resume (default: skip if last run
          succeeded)

      --no-squash-push
          Stop before `squash-push-bot` so it can be run manually

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

      --title <STR>
          Commit title (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

      --body <STR>
          Commit body (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

  -y, --yes
          Auto-approve interactive prompts (review gate, message-edit
          confirmation). Required when `--title` / `--body` aren't both supplied
          in non-interactive contexts

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

## Stage: trapezoid close-out

The close-out commit becomes a two-parent merge — first
parent the pre-cycle base (the parent of the ladder's first
commit), second parent the ladder tip (`-X`), the
`git merge --no-ff` convention — so
`git log --first-parent main` reads one commit per cycle
while the full ladder stays reachable via the second parent.

- The merge itself is trivial in-process: a two-parent
  commit in one transaction; no conflicts possible since the
  base is an ancestor of the tip.
- The real work is ochid stamping — the bot commit carries
  one ochid per work commit in the cycle (the AGENTS.md
  merge non-ff shape) while push today stamps only the
  topmost commit.
- Teach `validate-desc` + the push sanity verifiers the new
  legal shape (two parents, N ochids).
- Status: the 0.72.0 attempt to pull this stage forward
  paused on the `support-trapezoid-commits` bookmark and is
  now abandoned as a version — see the
  [parked-branch disposition](#parked-0720-branch-disposition--quarry-not-base)
  (its ladder plan remains the template for this cycle).
  The stage runs here, in program order, on the refactored
  internals, with body-intro validation as its first rung.
  The former enabler Todo "vc-x1 push: pause point between
  commit and publish stages" was retired unimplemented —
  native merge support supersedes the pause.

Design points settled in the 2026-07-20 session (the parked
cycle's planning):

- `--merge [<base>]`, opt-in per push, never automatic —
  the trapezoid is a first-party shape the user chooses at
  push time. Base is the merge's first parent (the parent
  of the task's first commit):
  - branch style (task on a feature bookmark, target
    sitting at the base): base defaults to the target
    bookmark's position
  - main style (task grew on the target, bookmark at the
    work tip): base can't be inferred — the explicit
    `<base>` revision is required
- The merge step sits after commit-bot, before
  bookmark-set — chids survive the rebase, so both ochid
  directions are injected normally and stay valid.
- Preconditions: base is a proper ancestor of the work
  tip; close-out has exactly one parent pre-rebase; target
  bookmark at the base or the work tip — anything else is
  divergence (e.g. a second repo instance moved the
  target): reconcile first.
- Both styles publish forward — the old bookmark position
  is one of the merge's parents, so the push never forces.
  Post-hoc conversion of an already-published close-out
  stays the manual `--ignore-immutable` recipe.
- ochid list: one `ochid:` per work commit the push newly
  publishes; whether to skip commits covered by an interim
  1:1 push is decided at implementation (bot-journal
  trailer scan exists in `squash_push::extract_ochids`).
- No state-file growth: `--merge` is per-invocation,
  re-passed on resume (see
  [stateless push](#stage-stateless-push)).
- Docs ride-along: the two trapezoid variants —
  committer-owned (close-out *is* the merge; this flag) vs
  PR-style (the integrator authors the merge; needs no
  vc-x1 machinery) — and why merge-commit integration,
  never squash/rebase, preserves chids and thus ochids
  (forks-multi-user.md owns the detail).

## Stage: por → dual conversion

Reviewed — here's the technique as the record describes it, applied to this cycle.

First, a correction to what I said earlier: I called a merge here "degenerate" because the rungs sit linearly under the base. That was wrong — 0.74.0 and 0.75.0 had exactly the same shape (base an ancestor of the ladder tip). That *is* the `git merge --no-ff` shape, and the refactor doc says so explicitly: "no conflicts possible since the base is an ancestor of the tip" (notes/refactor-20260716.md:418).

**The two revisions**

- base (`<prev>`, first parent) = `rmwlryuu docs: refactor program ladder + conventions` — the parent of the ladder's first rung (`yutlulms chore: open repo registry cycle`), i.e. the trunk position when the cycle opened.
- ladder tip (second parent) = `quuxksqw refactor: de-gitify init`.

This is the "main style" case from the design notes (notes/refactor-20260716.md:445): the cycle grew on the target bookmark itself, so the base can't be inferred and must be named explicitly.

**Where the manual step goes.** The key insight recorded at notes/refactor-20260716.md:449 — the merge is set up **after `commit-bot`, before `bookmark-set`**. Both repos are already committed and ochid-stamped at that point, and rebasing the close-out rewrites its SHA but *not* its change ID, so both ochid directions stay valid. That's what 0.74.0 did: "set up manually, published via `vc-x1 push --from bookmark-set`" (notes/chores/chores-14.md:290).

So the sequence:

1. `vc-x1-dev push refactor-vc-x1 --title … --body …` — runs preflight, review, message, `commit-work`, `commit-bot`, and must be **stopped before `bookmark-set`**.
2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto rmwlryuu --onto quuxksqw` — the close-out becomes the two-parent merge. `@` (the empty commit push left on top) gets re-parented back onto `quuxksqw` by `-r` semantics.
3. `jj new <merge>` — puts the empty `@` back above the merge, so `@-` is the merge.
4. `vc-x1-dev push --from bookmark-set` — resumes with saved state: work bookmark → merge, bot `main` → its `@-`, then `push-work`, `squash-push-bot`.

Both parents are already-published positions, so step 4 pushes forward — no force.

1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
7	the conversation — code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
8	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
9	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
10	equivalents — this project's manifest is recorded in
11	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
12	
13	## Cycles
14	
15	A cycle has three phases:
16	
17	- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's
18	  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
19	  it and starts at `-1` — see
20	  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
21	  cycle:
22	  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
23	    and the suffix scheme are project-specific — see
24	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
25	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
26	    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
27	    statement + plan ladder).
28	  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
29	- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) — the
30	  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
31	  needs; each runs through the
32	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
33	- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's
34	  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
35	  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
36	    `## Done`.
37	  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
38	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
39	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
40	    changed.
41	
42	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
43	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
44	result must always be published at close-out. See
45	[Pushing](#pushing).
46	
47	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
48	warrant its own ladder, it subdivides — `X.Y.Z-3.0`
49	Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
50	Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
51	at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
52	suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
53	for the local-ladder mechanics.
54	
55	## Chores sections
56	
57	A **chores section** is a `##` section in
58	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
59	general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
60	should have a reference to it on a `Commits:` list in a
61	chores file.
62	
63	The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
64	`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
65	with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`),
66	followed by an **empty `Commits:`** line. **Each work commit
67	then appends its own As-built rung + narrative note as it
68	lands** — the chores record is built up per commit, not held
69	back and written all at once at close-out; close-out only
70	*finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
71	`## In Progress` block). The `Commits:` line is backfilled
72	later, once the commit is permanent (see
73	[Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
74	
75	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
76	design subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in
77	AGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).
78	
79	### Commits backfill
80	
81	A chores section's `Commits:` line cites the commit(s) it
82	records, by SHA — but a SHA isn't stable until the commit
83	lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
84	release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or
85	squash rewrites it on the way. So:
86	
87	- A chores section is **opened with an empty `Commits:`** line.
88	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
89	  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
90	  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
91	  push later: **each push backfills the `Commits:` of the
92	  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
93	  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands —
94	  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
95	  invalidate.
96	
97	Use `[[N]]` refs — several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one
98	section records multiple commits (a merge non-ff close-out) —
99	with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's `# References`
100	(format in AGENTS.md
101	[Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references)).
102	A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
103	deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
104	`git log --grep "<title>"`.
105	
106	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma — a
107	**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
108	close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
109	SHA must be permanent.
110	
111	## Preparation
112	
113	The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
114	setup (a lightweight cycle omits it — see
115	[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):
116	
117	- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
118	  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
119	  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
120	  project-specific — see [versioning.md](versioning.md).
121	- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
122	  `## In Progress` and the todo item should have:
123	  - A **bold title line** — that will be the chores
124	    section header, minus the `## ` prefix.
125	  - A **succinct problem statement**; add if one is needed
126	  - A **plan ladder**.
127	- **Open the [chores section](#chores-sections)** —
128	  append a `##` header with the title it records — the
129	  cycle's anticipated close-out title.
130	
131	## Work-N
132	
133	The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …)
134	implement the change. As many as needed:
135	
136	- Each commit runs through the
137	  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
138	- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
139	  visibility).
140	- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
141	  [Pushing](#pushing)).
142	- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
143	  scope grows enough (see
144	  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).
145	
146	## Close-out
147	
148	The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`) does bookkeeping
149	only — the commit body describes that bookkeeping, not
150	what happens post-squash:
151	
152	- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a
153	  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.
154	- **Finalize the chores section** (opened during Preparation
155	  and grown per commit — see [Chores sections](#chores-sections)):
156	  - The problem statement is already the chores intro (written
157	    when the section was opened) and the plan ladder is already
158	    the `### As-built ladder` (a rung appended per commit), so
159	    close-out only *finalizes*, it does not cut-and-paste.
160	  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title if the
161	    cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor back-reference.
162	  - Add any `### design subsections`; optional `### Outcome`
163	    notes.
164	  - Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block with
165	    `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
166	- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
167	  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).
168	
169	Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
170	publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time —
171	see [Pushing](#pushing).
172	
173	## Numbering
174	
175	Each commit's phase is encoded in the version suffix — `-0`
176	Preparation, `-1`/`-2`/… Work, bare `X.Y.Z` Close-out,
177	recursively for sub-cycles. The full scheme — disambiguation,
178	nesting, optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
179	format, and the per-phase bump — lives in
180	[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering), which is the
181	single source of truth for this repo's versioning.
182	
183	## Per-commit flow

185	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
186	through:

content.text:
Thoughts only — no edits.

## Where the steps already live

Three places, each holding a fragment, and their disagreements are exactly what made me hesitate:

- **`notes/cycle-protocol.md` § Merge non-ff recipe** (~394–421) — the operator's how-to: the three jj steps we just ran. This is the closest thing to a canonical recipe.
- **`notes/refactor-20260716.md` § Stage: trapezoid close-out** (407–473) — the implementation design for `--merge [<base>]`: stage placement, the two base-inference styles, preconditions, the ochid-list question, `validate-desc` teaching.
- **`notes/chores/chores-14.md`** 0.74.0 close-out rung (~290) — the one-line as-built: "set up manually, published via `vc-x1 push --from bookmark-set`". This is the only record that the manual variant exists at all, and it's a passing mention inside a rung.

## The four things that were wrong or missing

Not "underspecified" — three are actively misleading, which is why I stopped to ask rather than just run it.

1. **The base rule contradicts itself across docs.** The recipe glosses `<prev>` as "the previous cycle's close-out (the current `main` tip)". The design doc says "the parent of the ladder's first commit". Those coincide on a branch-style cycle and *differed here*: previous close-out was `dc14a42` (facade), but the correct base was `eb4a12e`, the 0.75.1 docs interlude. Following the recipe's gloss literally would have swallowed that interlude into the merge's second-parent side and broken the one-commit-per-cycle first-parent reading. The design doc's phrasing is the right one; the recipe's gloss should be deleted, not reconciled.

2. **Recipe step 2's stated reason is factually wrong.** It says `jj new` is needed because "the rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted." That is not what `-r` does. What actually happened: `@` was re-parented onto the merge's *old* parent (`quuxksqw`) and sat off to the side, with the working tree reverting to pre-close-out content. Same corrective step, completely different reason — and the wrong reason makes the step look cosmetic when it's load-bearing (`bookmark-set` reads `@-`).

3. **The immutability caveat is over-broad.** "If the cycle was already pushed Keep separate its commits are immutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the push force-updates `main`." We rebased an already-pushed commit with no flag and no force complaint, because immutability keys on `trunk()` — `refactor-vc-x1` isn't it. The caveat is true for a close-out already on `main`; it should say so.

4. **The two orderings are never distinguished.** The design doc specifies the merge *in-flight* (after `commit-bot`, before `bookmark-set`). What we ran was *post-hoc-within-branch*: full push, reshape, re-push. Both are legal; only the first is what `--merge` will do. Undocumented, the recipe reads as if there's one procedure.

And the operational details nowhere recorded: the state file clears on completion, so the resume needs the bookmark passed positionally; `--no-squash-push` is what hands the bot repo back to you; and jj does **not** simplify the second parent away when the base is an ancestor of the tip — three cycles of evidence now, and it's the failure mode that would fail silently.

## The wart that belongs in the docs

Post-hoc reshaping publishes a SHA that then becomes unreachable. `af931b81` went to the remote at step 1 and was abandoned at step 4; the bookmark moved sideways, not forward. The design doc's "both styles publish forward — the push never forces" is a claim about the *in-flight* variant only. Two consequences worth writing down: anyone who fetched between step 1 and step 4 holds a dangling commit, and **no `Commits:` backfill may read a SHA in that window**. That's a real trap given the per-push backfill cadence — it's precisely when a backfill would otherwise be due.

## As an implementation spec

Today's run is a clean spec for `--merge` because it exercised every mechanism the flag needs, just with a human between the stages. What it settles:

- The in-flight ordering is achievable entirely inside push's state machine — the rebase and `jj new` slot between `commit-bot` and `bookmark-set`, before any remote contact, so the flag's version has neither the unreachable SHA nor the sideways move. The manual recipe's wart is an artifact of the flag not existing.
- Chid stability is confirmed end-to-end: trailers stamped at `commit-work`/`commit-bot` survived the rewrite in both directions, which is the premise the stage placement rests on.
- The preconditions to enforce in code are now concrete: base a proper ancestor of the tip, close-out single-parent pre-rebase, bookmark at base or tip, and — new — assert two parents *after* the rebase rather than trusting jj not to simplify.

## On README

Agreed in principle, with a sequencing caveat: README documents what the tool does, and `--merge` doesn't exist yet. Writing the trapezoid section into README now would document vapor. I'd write the corrected mechanics into `notes/` now and land the README section *with* the 0.79.0 implementation, where it's a ride-along on the same commit that makes it true.

On placement, to avoid a fourth copy: cycle-protocol owns the manual recipe (it's the operator doc, and it fans out to the template family); the refactor stage keeps only what's implementation-specific and points at the recipe; README later describes the flag's user-facing behavior. One canonical description each, cross-linked.

## Sequencing

This is a docs cycle, and there's precedent: 0.75.1 was exactly this — a planning/docs interlude between cycles. A **0.76.1** interlude would carry these corrections plus the 0.76.0 `Commits:` backfill (now safe, since the SHA is final at `71611891`), leaving 0.77.0 to open clean on split-push. The alternative — riding it into 0.77.0-0 — mixes an unrelated correction into a cycle-opening commit.

**The plain version:** the steps we ran are written down in three places, but two of them say things that are wrong, and the one detail that would silently ruin the result — whether the merge really keeps two parents — isn't mentioned at all. I'd fix those notes in a small docs cycle, use them as the build spec for the `--merge` flag later, and hold the README section until the flag actually exists.

content.text:
Thoughts only.

## Where the one definitive set should live

`notes/cycle-protocol.md` § the trapezoid recipe. It's the operator's how-to, it's the doc that fans out to the template family, and it survives the `--merge` flag (post-hoc conversion and non-vc-x1 projects still need hand steps). Everything else becomes a pointer.

That gives a clean rule for what each site keeps:

- **cycle-protocol** — *the* procedure: the four steps we ran, base rule, the two-parent assertion, the consequences. Nothing about implementation.
- **refactor-20260716.md § trapezoid stage** — implementation deltas only: base *inference* (branch vs main style), why the flag does it in-flight, preconditions as code checks, the ochid-list decision, `validate-desc` teaching, no-state-growth. Its restated mechanics ("the merge itself is trivial", "no conflicts since base is an ancestor") get deleted and replaced by a link. This section is also *ephemeral* — it becomes history when 0.79.0 ships — which is the strongest argument it must not own the canonical steps.
- **chores-14 rungs** — untouched. They're as-built records of their own commits, not spec.
- **README** — nothing yet; lands with the flag.

## Which ordering is the definitive one

The four-step post-hoc-within-branch we just ran. Not the in-flight ordering — that's a property of the future flag. In-flight is *technically* reachable today via `--step`'s interactive gates, but documenting two procedures is exactly the fragmentation you're asking to remove, and the non-interactive four-step is the one with three cycles of evidence behind it. So: one procedure, and the stage doc notes the flag will move the merge earlier and thereby drop the wart.

## What gets deleted, not just corrected

- The `<prev>` gloss ("the previous cycle's close-out / current `main` tip") — replaced by the parent-of-first-rung rule, which is the only correct one.
- Step 2's rationale about `@` being left *on* the merge — wrong mechanism, replaced by the real one (`-r` re-parents descendants onto the old parent).
- The blanket `--ignore-immutable` caveat — scoped to "close-out already on `trunk()`".
- "Set up squash/merge **before** invoking `vc-x1 push`" in § Shape at close-out push — a fifth site, and now simply false for the trapezoid.

## Two consolidations you may not have in view

**Vocabulary.** The docs carry two names for one thing: the option is called "Merge non-ff (current default)", the recipe "Merge non-ff recipe", and the prose says "trapezoid" everywhere else. You consistently say trapezoidal. I'd make **trapezoid** primary and keep "(merge non-ff)" as the one-time git-level gloss, renaming the option in the shape list to match. Single name, or the grep never finds all of it.

**AGENTS.md's ochid claim.** It says more than one ochid "occurs on a Merge non-ff close-out (one ochid per Work commit in the cycle)". Our trapezoid carried exactly **one**, because the rungs were pushed 1:1 as they landed. The rule is per-*push*, not per-cycle — AGENTS.md states that correctly one sentence earlier and then muddies it. Small scope fix, but it's a fourth site making a claim about trapezoids.

And the backlog has an entry asking for an ASCII drawing of the trapezoidal merge (`notes/todo-backlog.md` ~24) plus an older one about push setting up the non-FF shape (~31). The first is worth satisfying *inside the recipe* — a five-line diagram of base / ladder / merge kills the base-selection ambiguity permanently — and the second looks superseded by Todo #3, so the interlude can retire it.

## Shape of the cycle

Precedent is 0.75.1: a single commit, no ladder, no `-0`. I'd do the same — **`docs: trapezoid close-out recipe`**, one commit, with riders:

- the 0.76.0 `Commits:` backfill (safe now — `71611891` is final) and the program ladder's `[[N]]` for 0.76.0;
- a line on the 0.76.0 As-built close-out rung recording that it published as a trapezoid via the manual four-step;
- the backlog retirements above.

Two open questions I'd want settled before writing:

1. **chores-14 or chores-15?** chores-14 is past 800 lines and its intro frames it around the `support-trapezoid-commits` era. I don't know this project's roll-over rule — if it's era-based, an interlude that finally pins the trapezoid procedure is a reasonable place to close 14 and open 15; if it's size-based, it's overdue either way. Your call.
2. **Does the recipe belong to the shared protocol or to vc-x1?** cycle-protocol fans out to the template family, and the four steps name `vc-x1-dev push --from bookmark-set`. The jj half is universal; the push half is tool-specific. I'd write the steps in jj terms with the vc-x1 invocation called out as this project's binding, so the fan-out doesn't carry a tool other projects lack.

# Notes

This directory contains various notes and documentation related to the project.
Each file is organized by topic for easy reference.

By default there are the chores-NN.md files in
[chores/](chores). Chores are general notes about tasks;
short term tasks and their status live at the repo root in
[../TODO.md](../TODO.md). The chores-NN files are numbered
in sequence; the highest-numbered file is the active one,
older ones are closed.

Tool architecture — the CLI-args / `Context`+`Params` split, a
generic module map, the subcommand model, and what the
Context+Params port and the options_flags extraction *are* (the
*live status* is in the chores files) — lives at the repo root in
[`../ARCHITECTURE.md`](../ARCHITECTURE.md).

Multi-cycle programs too big for a TODO.md entry get their own
dated plan file — e.g.
[refactor-20260716.md](refactor-20260716.md) (typed jj facade →
jj-lib in-process): one `##` section per stage, so chores and
todo entries can reference a stage by anchor. The plan file owns
the forward design; chores still records each shipped cycle.

In the future we I expect we may want to create a "notes"
database to better manage the information, TBD.

Examples chore file:
```
# Chores-01.md
 
General maintenance tasks and considerations for the project see other files for
more specific topics. A chore in a chores file provides quick information on the
how and why of a particular chore.

## Create a binary that lists jj info 

This binary should list the changeID, commitID, and description title
and using `jj-lib`
```

## Workflow and conventions

Bot-facing workflow and conventions live in
[`../AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md):

- [Notes file conventions](../AGENTS.md#notes-file-conventions)
  — Todo format, Reference numbering, Notes references
  (`[[N]]` citation style), Markdown anchor links, Retiring
  Done entries.
- [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions) —
  section headers / Done entries exact-title rule, content
  rules, `Commits:` line format.
- [Code Conventions](../AGENTS.md#code-conventions) — doc
  comments, `// OK: …` on `unwrap*` calls, ask-on-ambiguity,
  stuck detection.

Per-cycle workflow lives in
[`cycle-protocol.md`](cycle-protocol.md):

- [Cycles](cycle-protocol.md#cycles) — three-phase shape
  (Preparation → Work → Close-out), `X.Y.Z-N` numbering,
  sub-cycles.
- [Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow) —
  cargo cycle (`fmt` / `clippy` / `test` / `install`),
  work + commit description review gates.
- [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description)
  — Conventional Commits + `(version)` suffix; body shape
  per work vs bot repo.
- [Pushing](cycle-protocol.md#pushing) — push policy,
  close-out shape, `.claude` cadence.

# Chores-15

Continuation of `chores-14.md` (closed at `0.76.0`, the
repo-registry close-out). This file covers `0.76.1` onward —
the remainder of the jj refactor program
([refactor-20260716.md](../refactor-20260716.md)) — worked on
the `refactor-vc-x1` bookmark while `main` parks at the
`0.71.0` tip.

Reference numbering is file-local — see
[`AGENTS.md`](../../AGENTS.md#reference-numbering); chores-15
starts at `[1]`.

## docs: trapezoid close-out recipe

Commits:

Publishing `0.76.0` as a trapezoid [[1]] needed four steps that
no single document described. The procedure was spread across
three places — the cycle-protocol recipe, the refactor doc's
trapezoid stage, and a passing mention in a `0.74.0` As-built
rung — and where they overlapped they disagreed. Two of the
three stated mechanisms were wrong, and the one check that
would catch a silent failure appeared nowhere. This interlude
consolidates them into a single definitive procedure before
the `--merge` flag is built from it.

- The four corrections, each a claim that survived because
  nothing was the source of truth:
  - **Base selection.** The recipe glossed the first parent
    as "the previous cycle's close-out (the current `main`
    tip)"; the design doc said "the parent of the ladder's
    first commit". They coincide only when no interlude sits
    between cycles. At `0.76.0` they differed — the base was
    the `0.75.1` docs interlude, not the `0.75.0` close-out —
    and the recipe's gloss would have swallowed the interlude
    into the merge's ladder side.
  - **Why `jj new` is needed.** The recipe attributed it to
    the rebase leaving `@` *on* the merge. It doesn't:
    `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants onto the rebased
    commit's **old** parent, so `@` lands beside the merge,
    not on it. Same step, different reason — and the wrong
    reason makes a load-bearing step read as cosmetic, since
    `bookmark-set` resolves `@-`.
  - **Immutability.** "Its commits are immutable, the rebase
    needs `--ignore-immutable`" is true only when the
    close-out is already on `trunk()`. A long-lived topic
    bookmark isn't, so the reshape needs no flag.
  - **Ordering.** The design doc specifies the merge in-flight
    (after `commit-bot`, before `bookmark-set`); the four-step
    manual procedure reshapes after a completed push. Both are
    legal, they have different consequences, and nothing said
    so.
- The missing check: jj does **not** collapse the second
  parent when the base is an ancestor of the tip, but nothing
  said to verify it. A simplified merge is indistinguishable
  from a correct one in `jj log --no-graph`, and the mistake
  is only visible once published. The recipe now asserts the
  parent count explicitly. Observed intact across `0.74.0`,
  `0.75.0`, and `0.76.0`.
- Consolidation, one home each:
  - `cycle-protocol.md` owns the procedure — it is the
    operator's how-to and it outlives the flag (post-hoc
    conversion and non-vc-x1 projects still need hand steps).
    The jj steps are written in jj terms with the `vc-x1 push`
    invocations called out as this project's binding, so the
    template-family fan-out doesn't carry a tool other
    projects lack.
  - The refactor doc's
    [trapezoid stage](../refactor-20260716.md#stage-trapezoid-close-out)
    keeps only what is implementation-specific and links to
    the recipe. It is ephemeral — it becomes history when the
    flag ships — which is the reason it must not own the
    steps.
  - `README.md` gets the user-facing description **with** the
    flag, not before: documenting `--merge` while it doesn't
    exist would be documenting vapor.
- Vocabulary collapsed to one word. The shape was "merge
  non-ff" in the option list and section headers, "trapezoid"
  in every other paragraph. **Trapezoid** is now primary, with
  "(merge non-ff)" as a one-time git-level gloss, so a grep
  finds all of it.
- The published-then-reshaped wart is now written down: step
  4 moves the bookmark sideways, so step 1's SHA becomes
  unreachable and anyone who fetched in between holds a
  dangling commit. The consequence that bites this project is
  the backfill embargo — a `Commits:` fill must never read a
  SHA from that window, which is exactly when the per-push
  cadence would otherwise be due.

### As-built riders

- `AGENTS.md` ochid scoping: "more than one occurs on a merge
  non-ff close-out (one ochid per Work commit in the cycle)"
  overstated the rule. The count is per **push** — `0.76.0`'s
  trapezoid carried exactly one, because its rungs were
  published 1:1 as they landed. The preceding sentence already
  said this correctly; the trailing gloss now agrees with it.
- Backlog retirements: the trapezoidal-merge diagram entry is
  satisfied by the diagram in the recipe (a better home than
  the proposed `notes/README.md` — it sits where the base is
  chosen), and the `vc-x1 push --merge` entry is superseded by
  the ranked `TODO.md` trapezoid-close-out entry.
- `0.76.0` backfill: the close-out `Commits:` ref in
  chores-14's As-built ladder, the program ladder's rung in
  `TODO.md`, and a note on that rung recording it as the first
  trapezoid published by the four-step procedure.

# References

[1]: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/71611891f67a "71611891f67a34f5e11a344ffe4e439ace93750f"

- **Still transparent** — report each commit/push as it lands
  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
- **When in doubt, ask** — ambiguous authorization falls back to
  per-push approval.

### Shape at close-out push

At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
the options and get user approval before pushing — once on
the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
needs approval), so choose deliberately.

- **Squash to one commit** — single entry on the target.
  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
  focused on one or two files.
- **Merge non-ff** *(current default)* — `main` gains a
  merge commit (`X.Y.Z`); cycle commits stay reachable via
  two parents. `jj log -r ..@ -n <N>` shows the trapezoidal
  shape. See [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe)
  for the full setup sequence.
- **Keep separate** — one commit per cycle entry on
  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
  `Commits:` ref; no consolidation churn.

Set up squash/merge before invoking `vc-x1 push`; use
`jj git push` directly for non-standard shapes.

### Merge non-ff recipe

Setting up a [Merge non-ff](#shape-at-close-out-push)
close-out is a fixed sequence. `<closeout>` is the cycle's
close-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out
(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last
Work commit:

1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge** — `jj rebase -r
   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.
   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.
   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).
   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.

   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of
   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.
2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the
   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing
   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;
   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.
3. **Push** — `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.

**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are
immutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the
push force-updates `main`.
The standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*
the close-out push.

### vc-x1 push wrapper

### Merge non-ff recipe

Setting up a [Merge non-ff](#shape-at-close-out-push)
close-out is a fixed sequence. `<closeout>` is the cycle's
close-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out
(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last
Work commit:

1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge** — `jj rebase -r
   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.
   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.
   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).
   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.

   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of
   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.
2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the
   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing
   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;
   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.
3. **Push** — `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.

**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are
immutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the
push force-updates `main`.
The standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*
the close-out push.

### Trapezoid close-out recipe

A [trapezoid](#shape-at-close-out-push) close-out is
published in four steps: an ordinary close-out push, a
two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the
bookmark at the reshaped commit.

```
  main line   …──<base>──────────────────<closeout>──
                    \                    /
  ladder             <rung-1>──…──<tip>─┘
```

- `<base>` — the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
  is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
  first parent.
- `<tip>` — the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
  second parent.
- `<closeout>` — the close-out commit, created by step 1.

The steps, with this project's `vc-x1` binding first and the
underlying jj beneath it:

1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "…" --body "…"` — the
   ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
   `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>` —
   `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
   argument order.
3. `jj new <closeout>` — puts an empty `@` above the merge.
4. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --from bookmark-set
   --no-squash-push` — advances the bookmark to the reshaped
   `@-` and publishes it, leaving the bot repo to a separate
   `vc-x1 squash-push`.

Steps 2–4 are `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` +
`jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .` for a project
without vc-x1; the jj half is the portable part.

#### Details

- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
  `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
  once published.
- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
  and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
  rung, not the last close-out.
- **Step 3 is load-bearing.** `jj rebase -r` re-parents
  descendants onto the rebased commit's **old** parent, so
  the empty `@` left by step 1 ends up beside the merge, not
  on it — and `bookmark-set` resolves `@-`. Skipping step 3
  advances the bookmark to the wrong revision.
- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
  becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
  [`Commits:` backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
  SHA from that window — wait until step 4 lands.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
  push force-updates the target.
- **Step 4 needs the bookmark named.** A completed push
  clears its state file, so pass `<bookmark>` positionally
  rather than relying on a resume.

#### Recovery

- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3** — the local
  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.
  Do not push a shape you did not intend — after step 4 the
  remote boundary is crossed and recovery is forward-only.
- **Bookmark advanced to the wrong revision** (step 3
  skipped): `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` before
  pushing. If step 4 already pushed it, the fix is a second
  sideways move, not a rewrite.

## Stage: trapezoid close-out

`push --merge [<base>]` builds the trapezoid itself, replacing
the four-step manual procedure. The shape, the base rule, and
the manual steps are specified once in
[the recipe](cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) —
this section covers only what implementing the flag adds.

- The merge itself is trivial in-process: a two-parent commit
  in one transaction; no conflicts possible since the base is
  an ancestor of the tip.
- Doing it **in-flight** (see the stage placement below) is
  strictly better than the manual procedure: nothing is
  published in the interim shape, so there is no unreachable
  SHA, no sideways bookmark move, and no backfill embargo
  window. That wart is an artifact of the flag not existing.
- Teach `validate-desc` + the push sanity verifiers the new
  legal shape (two parents, N ochids).
- Assert the parent count **after** the rebase rather than
  trusting jj not to simplify the edge — the manual recipe's
  verification step, promoted to a code check.
- Status: the 0.72.0 attempt to pull this stage forward
  paused on the `support-trapezoid-commits` bookmark and is
  now abandoned as a version — see the
  [parked-branch disposition](#parked-0720-branch-disposition--quarry-not-base)
  (its ladder plan remains the template for this cycle).
  The stage runs here, in program order, on the refactored
  internals, with body-intro validation as its first rung.
  The former enabler Todo "vc-x1 push: pause point between
  commit and publish stages" was retired unimplemented —
  native merge support supersedes the pause.

Design points settled in the 2026-07-20 session (the parked
cycle's planning):

- `--merge [<base>]`, opt-in per push, never automatic —
  the trapezoid is a first-party shape the user chooses at
  push time. Base is the merge's first parent (the parent
  of the task's first commit):
  - branch style (task on a feature bookmark, target
    sitting at the base): base defaults to the target
    bookmark's position
  - main style (task grew on the target, bookmark at the
    work tip): base can't be inferred — the explicit
    `<base>` revision is required
- The merge step sits after commit-bot, before
  bookmark-set — chids survive the rebase, so both ochid
  directions are injected normally and stay valid.
- Preconditions: base is a proper ancestor of the work
  tip; close-out has exactly one parent pre-rebase; target
  bookmark at the base or the work tip — anything else is
  divergence (e.g. a second repo instance moved the
  target): reconcile first.
- Both styles publish forward — the old bookmark position
  is one of the merge's parents, so the push never forces.
  Post-hoc conversion of an already-published close-out
  stays the manual `--ignore-immutable` recipe.
- ochid list: one `ochid:` per work commit the push newly
  publishes; whether to skip commits covered by an interim
  1:1 push is decided at implementation (bot-journal
  trailer scan exists in `squash_push::extract_ochids`).
- No state-file growth: `--merge` is per-invocation,
  re-passed on resume (see
  [stateless push](#stage-stateless-push)).
- Docs ride-along: the two trapezoid variants —
  committer-owned (close-out *is* the merge; this flag) vs
  PR-style (the integrator authors the merge; needs no
  vc-x1 machinery) — and why merge-commit integration,
  never squash/rebase, preserves chids and thus ochids
  (forks-multi-user.md owns the detail).

16	1. **vc-x1 push: per-repo bookmark names.** Allow code-side
17	   and `.claude`-side bookmarks to differ; currently
18	   `.claude` is locked to `main` regardless of the
19	   app-side `<bookmark>`. Sibling generalization to the
20	   N:1 / `--squash` / `--merge` work — together they make
21	   push handle all close-out shapes with arbitrary
22	   bookmark layouts.
23	2. **Investigate `linkme` for subcommand registration.**
24	   Distributed-slice registry — each subcommand registers itself
25	   at link time; `main.rs` discovers them via the slice rather
26	   than matching a `Commands` enum. Reduces per-subcommand
27	   touchpoints from 3 (mod decl + enum variant + match arm) to 1
28	   (registration). Costs: loses compile-time exhaustiveness
29	   (missing registration = runtime gap); help-output ordering
30	   depends on link order unless sorted; macro-magic dependency.
31	   Revisit once the `0.50.0` trait sweep's per-arm cost has been
32	   felt under real "add a subcommand" load.
33	   <https://github.com/dtolnay/linkme>
34	3. **Investigate `inventory` as `linkme` alternative.** Same
35	   shape as `linkme` — runtime-iterable registry populated by
36	   `inventory::submit!` per subcommand. Trade-offs mirror
37	   linkme's. Pick one if/when the trait sweep's match becomes
38	   the felt bottleneck.
39	   <https://github.com/dtolnay/inventory>
40	4. **forks-multi-user + bot-data-formats follow-through.**
41	   Design captured across two notes; concrete work to
42	   land when a cycle picks it up. Major pieces:
43	   multi-line `ochid:` parser/emitter; bot-side
44	   immutability enforcement; URL-shaped ochid (per-user
45	   / cross-repo); vendor-subdir layout
46	   (`.bot/<vendor>/<version>/<id>.<ext>`) +
